This configuration was fixed from 2023 grouped cross-validation before any A2024 scoring. It is a labelled D-05 diagnostic and must not be adopted without the owner.
- Buildings: C0 unchanged.
- Contents: C0 unchanged.

summary: I measured how much written_premium adds to C0's ranking. The signal is x = log(premium / annual C0 rate), centred within year x channel x new-business cells. I tried it as a one-parameter offset, piecewise-linear, banded and XGBoost residual forms, choosing among them by 2023 cross-validation grouped by customer. Only motor showed a signal in 2023, and only on new business (+0.0123 on motor D2, consistent across folds), and it did not hold up on A2024. The configuration I fixed in advance (motor new-business split; buildings and contents left as C0) scores 0.11915 against C0's 0.12012 (gain -0.00096, 95% interval -0.0039 to +0.0033), and all six configurations scored are below C0. On this evidence, leaving written_premium out (D-05) costs no measurable ranking power, so D-05 should stand.

final_configuration:
"B_seg" (frozen in variation.py BASE/CONFIG, same for all three lines).
- Model: XGBoost reg:tweedie p = 1.5 on uncapped y_full with unit weights. base_margin = log(c0 x k), where k is the deviance-optimal emerging level of each training (year, new_business) cell. c0 already includes exposure (slope of log c0 on log exposure is 0.99-1.01), so this is the "y with base_margin including log exposure" form, and it matches the leaderboard's unweighted deviance on row totals.
- Hyperparameters: max_depth 2, eta 0.02, subsample 0.7, colsample_bytree 0.5, and one-vs-rest categorical splits (max_cat_to_onehot 1000). min_child_weight and lambda are each 3000 row-equivalents of the mean expected hessian at the offset. Labels and offsets are divided by mean(c0), so hessians are of order one. nthread 2, seed 2031.
- Tree count: five-fold customer-grouped CV on whatever train is passed, in 10-tree steps up to 500, minimising held-out level-matched deviance. If 0 trees is best, the line returns C0.
- Output: c0 x exp(f), re-anchored so that within new business and within renewals the training rows keep C0's total. The overall level and the new-business/renewal balance are left to the level-setting step.
- Fitted on 2023: 0 trees buildings (= C0), 50 trees contents, 0 trees motor (= C0). Fitted on 2023 + 2024 for 2025: 0 / 50 / 0 again.
- Features: 55 / 54 / 49 for buildings / contents / motor. Changes from the raw fields: log sum insured; tenure_years replaces customer_since_year; occupation cleaned; year_built set to missing where 1900 was imputed.
- How it was chosen: the hyperparameters ("B") had the best pooled CV gain of 24 configurations compared by CV on 2023 only. Segment anchoring was added after B was scored on A2024, so it is a selection made on A2024 and is counted.

summary: I fitted a heavily regularised XGBoost Tweedie (p = 1.5) residual on C0 using emerging fields only. The offset is log c0 plus the emerging level of each (year, new-business) cell, the tree count comes from five-fold customer-grouped CV, and the result is re-anchored so C0's new-business/renewal balance is unchanged. final_configuration:

All lines use XGBoost Tweedie p=1.5, depth 3, eta 0.1, subsample 0.8, colsample 0.8, lambda 1, min_child_weight = 5000 rows x the median per-row hessian, seed 3103 and nthread 2. Developed rows: every claim row plus 20% of claim-free rows, which are weighted 5. The offset is log(exposure_plain) + log(base rate) + meta slope x (year - 2024). Score rows are put at the prediction year, so 2025 = the training years' level x exp(slope x 1). The level L is the Tweedie-optimal scale of 4-fold out-of-fold predictions (folds by customer) on the emerging training rows. Per line:

- Motor: shared features, weight 1, target capped at 50,000 per row, 120 trees, GBM alone (a = 1.0).

final_configuration: Fixed by rules set on 2023 before any 2024 scoring (S4). summary: I built a two-stage frequency x severity model on the developed market using C0's portable features: a Poisson GLM for claim counts, a Gamma GLM for capped small-claim severity, and a compact Poisson GLM plus a mean-excess load for claims above 50k (buildings and motor). I then gave it separate emerging frequency, severity and large-loss levels, and optional ridge Poisson frequency corrections chosen by grouped cross-validation on 2023. None of the versions ranks emerging risks better than C0 on A2024: level-matched pooled D2 moves by between -0.0003 and +0.0003 and every interval spans zero. Any gain is level only: raw pooled D2 rises from 0.1100 to 0.1192 with the level-recalibrated version. The motor frequency correction chosen on 2023 did not carry over to 2024. The frozen configuration scores 0.11978 against C0's 0.12012, so I do not recommend adopting it for ranking.

final_configuration:
Frozen before any A2024 score (constants in variation.py): C0 times the missing-value neutralisation times a construction correction, then rebalanced to C0's total on the scored rows.
(1) Missing-value neutralisation: C0's average missing-value relativity for days_unoccupied, smoke_alarms, marital_status, household_size, years_at_address, distance_to_river_km, soil_type, roof_type and energy_rating is divided out. It is estimated without outcomes, by an exposure-weighted regression of log(C0 rate) on the nine missing indicators and year intercepts, over the training rows' features only. The relativities removed, fitted on 2023, are: river distance x1.098, soil x0.933, energy rating x1.051, roof x1.028, the rest within 1.2% of 1. Flood zone is excluded: about 3% missing in both markets, and informative in developed.
(2) Construction correction: a Tweedie p=1.5 GLM with the neutralised C0 as offset, unpenalised year intercepts, and ridge-penalised one-hot construction levels (lambda = 1e4) on the training target capped at 25,000 a row. The 2023 fit gives log coefficients brick -0.082, non_standard +0.191, stone +0.145, timber -0.254.
The cap was chosen by customer-grouped 5-fold x 5-seed cross-validation within 2023 (25k beat 10k, 50k and no cap). The penalty was deliberately set above the cross-validation optimum of 1e3 to guard against over-tuning.
Contents and motor return C0. No region, wildfire extrapolation, written_premium, gender, customer_since_year or customer_service_contacts.
Recommendation after A2024: do not adopt; keep buildings = C0.

summary: I refitted ridge-penalised offset Tweedie corrections on C0, with a year intercept and C0's level preserved. They were fitted on emerging 2023 targets capped at the 95th or 99th percentile or at the 50k large-claim threshold (rescaled to the uncapped total), with Huber down-weighting of extreme rows and forward selection, and every penalty and choice was made by customer-grouped CV on 2023. Capping made the corrections less harmful (factor-set S2: gain -0.0017 uncapped, -0.0001 capped at the 95th percentile) but never turned one into a gain, pooled or on any line apart from a negligible +0.0007 for contents. The corrections that 2023 CV liked most (motor new business, buildings age band, construction and region) were the most harmful in 2024. Those effects look year-specific, which a within-year CV cannot detect, so under the guard rule the frozen final configuration is C0 on all three lines.

final_configuration: Frozen in variation.py (FROZEN) before any A2024 scoring; it is not changed after seeing A2024. final_configuration:
Frozen as FINAL_CONFIG in variation.py and chosen only by CV within 2023 before any A2024 scoring.

Model: log mu = log c0 + intercept per (line, year) + grouped effects, fitted by penalised Tweedie p=1.5 (Fisher scoring). The ridge penalty k is in pseudo-claims.

Terms:
- buildings region: merged until every group has at least 100 claims, k=50.
- buildings construction_type: at least 50 claims per group, k=15.
- motor new_business: raw levels, k=50.
- motor fuel_type: at least 200 claims per group, k=500.
- Contents is unchanged (C0).

Merging: the group with the fewest claims joins the neighbour with the closest A/E against C0, smoothed by one pseudo-claim. For nominal factors, neighbours are taken in A/E order; for ordinal factors, in the factor's natural order. Merging is re-run inside each CV fold.

Selection rule, fixed before running:
- A factor was a candidate if its best single-factor CV gain was at least 0.0005 and positive on both fold seeds.
- Forward stepwise per line, adding a term only if it raised CV gain by at least 0.0003.
- All penalties then scaled by 0.5, 1 or 2, keeping the best (0.5).
- A pooled variant needed to beat the separate fit by at least 0.0003; none did.

Levels unseen in training get zero effect. For prediction, the line intercept is the training-exposure-weighted mean of its year intercepts.

summary:
Grouping sparse levels did not help. The configuration chosen by customer-grouped 5-fold cross-validation within 2023 (two fold seeds) scored worse than C0 on A2024: pooled level-matched D2 0.10079 against C0's 0.12012, a gain of -0.0193 (95% CI -0.0322 to -0.0080). Recommendation: do not adopt.

Within 2023 the CV gain was +0.0112 (SE 0.005), and +0.0110 on a third fold seed. That gain did not carry over to 2024.

Single-factor results:
- Data-driven merging helped in CV only for buildings region (two groups, CV +0.0037 against +0.0024 for raw levels), buildings construction and motor fuel.
- Merging nominal factors with many levels by their noisy actual-to-expected (A/E) made things worse. make_model fell to -0.0037 at 200 claims per group and -0.0053 at 400.
- A priori occupation grouping (80 raw spellings to 20 jobs) gave about zero or negative in every line. Porting the developed market's job relativities also gave about zero (+0.00003). Developed motor shows Manager at 1.69, but emerging 2023 shows 0.69.
- Motor new business (NB) was the strongest single correction (CV +0.0051). Age band x NB and channel x NB added nothing once NB was in.

Pooling across lines never beat fitting each line separately in CV. Tried: region shared by buildings and contents (with or without motor), NB shared across all three lines, and age band shared by the household lines. Each was tried as purely shared, shared with penalised line deviations, and shared times a line multiplier (kappa).

Why it failed, from 2023 rows only:
- Buildings region: claim frequency by region is flat (0.82 to 1.16). The cost split comes from large claims: E02 holds 4 of the top 10 claims, and capping at the 95th percentile moves E04 from 1.42 to 0.87.
- Motor NB: cost A/E is 1.81, but frequency is 1.38 and the capped A/E is 1.26. The fitted Tweedie relativity NB/renewal is 2.4x.

Customer-grouped CV within one year cannot detect this. A year's large claims and weather events recur across folds, so CV rewards fitting them. Grouping or correction work on this book needs a capped or frequency-based A/E, and a check that effects are stable from year to year.
